title: How does a token bucket let a burst through but refuse a flood?
checkedAgainst: golang.org/x/time/rate v0.15.0: the Go program in `oracle/` runs `rate.NewLimiter(r, 5).AllowN` on the explainer’s ten arrival times at one, two and four tokens a second, and `model.test.ts` holds the model’s answers and balances to `fixtures/token-bucket-xtime.json`, checks the model against an independent quarter-token ledger at varied rates and capacities, and the boundary below which R10 is refused; `scene.test.ts` holds the check answers to the model. This schedule only; not every feature of the Go package.

grounding.subject: Go’s golang.org/x/time/rate v0.15.0
grounding.label: Recorded: Go’s golang.org/x/time/rate v0.15.0
grounding.sentence: Checked against a recording made once, which the model’s tests compare with: Go’s golang.org/x/time/rate v0.15.0.

answer: A burst can spend only the tokens saved up, and only elapsed time adds more

questions.question: R6 is refused at all three rates. Would a faster refill or a bigger bucket let it through, and why?
questions.answer: A bigger bucket. R1 to R6 arrive at the same instant, so no time passes and refill adds nothing at any rate. A bucket of six tokens, still at 2 a second, answers R6 with 200.

questions.question: At 2 tokens a second, a client sends one request every 0.4 seconds from a full bucket and never pauses. Is any request refused, and what share gets through in the long run?
questions.answer: Yes. Each gap earns 0.8 tokens and each request spends one, so the saved five drain by 0.2 a request and request 22 is the first refused. From then on 80 of every 100 get through, 2 a second: the refill rate, however long the flood lasts.

questions.question: Suppose R10 arrived at 1.5 s instead of 5 s. At which of the three rates would it be refused?
questions.answer: At 1 token a second only. At 1 a second R9 leaves 0 and R10 finds 0.5; at 2 a second R9 leaves 0 and R10 finds 1; at 4 a second R9 leaves 1 and R10 finds 3. Half a second has to earn the token R9 did not leave.

scenarios.name: Refill per second: 1 token
invariants: the bucket stands where the balance line ends

steps.title: Ten requests from one client, and a bucket of five tokens
steps.line: Predict: R1–R6 arrive at the same instant. How many get 200?
steps.caption: A server limits each client: a request it serves gets 200, OK; one it refuses gets 429, Too Many Requests, telling the client to slow down. A short burst should still get through, so the server keeps the client a balance of at most five tokens: the bucket. Each accepted request spends one token; one that finds less than one, under the 1 token line, gets 429. Ten requests arrive at the times above their boxes.
steps.picture: “Bucket balance”, 4 labelled values; The bucket, filled to 5.0 of 5 tokens; A chart of tokens, 0 to 5, against time, 0 to 5 s, with a dashed line at the one token a request needs; Requests R1 to R10 at their arrival times: none answered yet; Code “bucket.allow(now), rate = 1”, 8 lines. Refill: 2: tokens = min(5; 3: tokens + (now - lastRefill) * rate); 4: lastRefill = now.

steps.title: Answer: five 200s, then a 429
steps.line: Predict: R7 arrives half a second later, at 0.5 s. 200 or 429?
steps.caption: No time passed between R1 and R6, so the line drops one token per request and R6 finds 0.0, under the 1 token line: 429. A burst can spend only the tokens saved up, and only elapsed time adds more. On each arrival the server adds elapsed time multiplied by the refill rate, here 1 token a second, before deciding whether to spend a token. The line between arrivals shows available credit; no background timer needs to update the balance.
steps.picture: “Bucket balance”, 4 labelled values; The bucket, filled to 0.0 of 5 tokens; A chart of the balance over time: it climbs at 1 a second between calls and drops one token for each 200. Dots mark what R1–R6 found; R6 at 0.0 is under the one-token line and got 429; Requests R1 to R10 at their arrival times: 5 answered 200, R6 429, 4 waiting; Code “bucket.allow(now), rate = 1”, 8 lines. Refuse: 5: if (tokens < 1) return 429. New in this step: Tokens left: 0; Accepted: 5; Rejected: R6; and 3 more.

steps.title: Answer: 429. R7 finds 0.5 tokens after half a second
steps.line: R8 at 1 s finds 1.0; R9 at the same instant finds what R8 left.
steps.caption: Between calls the line climbs 1 token a second. Half a second after the burst, R7 finds 0.5 tokens, less than the one a request needs, so it gets 429. The rate decides it: the same half second buys 0.5 tokens at 1 a second (429), 1.0 token at 2 a second (200) and 2.0 tokens at 4 a second (200). R7 (0.5) and R9 (0.0) are under the 1 token line, so they get 429.
steps.picture: “Bucket balance”, 4 labelled values; The bucket, filled to 0.0 of 5 tokens; A chart of the balance over time: it climbs at 1 a second between calls and drops one token for each 200. Dots mark what R1–R9 found; R6 at 0.0, R7 at 0.5 and R9 at 0.0 are under the one-token line and got 429; Requests R1 to R10 at their arrival times: 6 answered 200, R6, R7 and R9 429, 1 waiting; Code “bucket.allow(now), rate = 1”, 8 lines. Refuse: 5: if (tokens < 1) return 429. New in this step: Last refill (s): 1; Accepted: 6; Rejected: R6, R7, R9; and 2 more.

steps.title: R10 waits 4 s and finds 4 tokens
steps.line: The line climbs to 4.0, under the cap of five.
steps.caption: R9 left 0, and a wait of 4 s at 1 token a second brings the balance to 4, under min(5, …)'s cap. R10 spends one and leaves 3. At 2 tokens a second and 4 tokens a second the same wait would pass five, and min(5, …) would stop the balance there.
steps.picture: “Bucket balance”, 4 labelled values; The bucket, filled to 3.0 of 5 tokens; A chart of the balance over time: it climbs at 1 a second between calls and drops one token for each 200. Dots mark what R1–R10 found; R6 at 0.0, R7 at 0.5 and R9 at 0.0 are under the one-token line and got 429; Requests R1 to R10 at their arrival times: 7 answered 200, R6, R7 and R9 429; Code “bucket.allow(now), rate = 1”, 8 lines. Spend: 6: tokens -= 1; 7: return 200. New in this step: Tokens left: 3; Last refill (s): 5; Accepted: 7; and 3 more.

steps.title: The same ten requests at 1, 2 and 4 tokens a second
steps.line: 429s at 4 / s: R6; at 1 / s: R6, R7 and R9.
steps.caption: Each row runs the same ten requests at its rate; outlined: this scenario. Circles are 200s, crosses 429s. R6 is refused at every rate, since no time passes inside the burst, and R10 is accepted at every rate: after its 4-second wait it finds at least 4 tokens. Below a fifth of a token a second, R10 too would be refused. The bucket’s capacity sets the burst; its rate sets how soon the client can send again.
steps.picture: Requests R1 to R10, left to right. 1 / s: R6, R7 and R9 get 429; all other requests get 200. 2 / s: R6 and R9 get 429; all other requests get 200. 4 / s: R6 gets 429; all other requests get 200. The 1 / s row is outlined.
